claim: rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replicates rapidly and to high-titers (107 to 108 PFU/ml within 48 hr)
source: Notably, rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replicates rapidly and to high-titers (107 to 108 PFU/ml within 48 hr), mimics the SARS-CoV-2 requirement for ACE-2 as a receptor, and is neutralized by COVID19 convalescent plasma and SARS-CoV-2 S-specific human monoclonal antibodies (Schmidt et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of viral titers and timeframes, supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2020

claim: rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP mimics the SARS-CoV-2 requirement for ACE-2 as a receptor
source: Notably, rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replicates rapidly and to high-titers (107 to 108 PFU/ml within 48 hr), mimics the SARS-CoV-2 requirement for ACE-2 as a receptor, and is neutralized by COVID19 convalescent plasma and SARS-CoV-2 S-specific human monoclonal antibodies (Schmidt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by reference to prior work (Schmidt et al., 2020)

claim: rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP is neutralized by COVID19 convalescent plasma and SARS-CoV-2 S-specific human monoclonal antibodies
source: Notably, rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replicates rapidly and to high-titers (107 to 108 PFU/ml within 48 hr), mimics the SARS-CoV-2 requirement for ACE-2 as a receptor, and is neutralized by COVID19 convalescent plasma and SARS-CoV-2 S-specific human monoclonal antibodies (Schmidt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by reference to prior work (Schmidt et al., 2020)

claim: The mutation rate of VSV is ~ 10−4 to 10−5/base per replication cycle
source: Because the mutation rate of VSV is ~ 10−4 to 10−5/base per replication cycle (Steinhauer and Holland, 1986; Steinhauer et al., 1989; Combe and Sanjuán, 2014), we estimated that this procedure should generate a large fraction of the possible replication-competent mutants within a population size of 1 × 106.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies on VSV mutation rates

claim: Infection with rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP in the presence of the monoclonal antibodies C121 or C144 reduced the number of infectious units from 106 to a few hundred
source: Infection with rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP in the presence of the monoclonal antibodies C121 or C144 reduced the number of infectious units from 106 to a few hundred, as estimated by the frequency of GFP-positive cells (Figure 1B) a reduction of > 1000 fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1B showing GFP-positive cells

claim: C135 reduced infection by ~ 100 fold
source: C135 reduced infection by ~ 100 fold.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the selection experiments

claim: Mutations E484K and Q493K/R within the RBD were present at high frequencies in both p2 selected populations in the presence of C121
source: In the case of C121, mutations E484K and Q493K/R within the RBD were present at high frequencies in both p2 selected populations, with mutation at a proximal position (F490L) present in one p2 population (Figure 2A, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and Table 2

claim: Viruses passaged in the presence of monoclonal antibody C144 had mutations at positions E484 and Q493, but not at F490
source: Viruses passaged in the presence of monoclonal antibody C144 also had mutations at positions E484 and Q493, but not at F490 (Figure 2C, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and Table 2

claim: Virus populations passaged in the presence of monoclonal antibody C135 had mutations R346K/S/L and N440K at high frequency
source: In contrast, virus populations passaged in the presence of monoclonal antibody C135 lacked mutations at E484 or Q493, and instead had mutations R346K/S/L and N440K at high frequency (Figure 2C, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and Table 2

claim: Mutations outside the RBD, specifically at N148S, K150R/E/T/Q and S151P in the N-terminal domain (NTD) were present at modest frequency in COV-47 p2 cultures and became more abundant at p3 and p4
source: Conversely, mutations outside the RBD, specifically at N148S, K150R/E/T/Q and S151P in the N-terminal domain (NTD) were present at modest frequency in COV-47 p2 cultures and became more abundant at p3 and p4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and Table 2

claim: Virus populations passaged in the presence of COV-NY plasma had mutations within RBD encoding sequence (K444R/N/Q and V445E) that were abundant at p2
source: Specifically, virus populations passaged in the presence of COV-NY plasma had mutations within RBD encoding sequence (K444R/N/Q and V445E) that were abundant at p2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and Table 2

claim: Each of the isolated rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP mutants replicated with similar kinetics to the parental rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP1D7 and rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP2E1 viruses
source: Notably, each of the isolated rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP mutants replicated with similar kinetics to the parental rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP1D7 and rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP2E1 viruses (Figure 3A), suggesting that the mutations that emerged during replication in the presence of monoclonal antibodies or plasma did not confer a substantial loss of fitness, at least in the context of rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The mutations that emerged during replication in the presence of monoclonal antibodies or plasma did not confer a substantial loss of fitness, at least in the context of rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP
source: Notably, each of the isolated rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP mutants replicated with similar kinetics to the parental rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP1D7 and rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP2E1 viruses (Figure 3A), suggesting that the mutations that emerged during replication in the presence of monoclonal antibodies or plasma did not confer a substantial loss of fitness, at least in the context of rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP.
evidence: This is inferred from the replication kinetics data shown in Figure 3A

claim: For mutants in RBD sequences that arose in the C121, C135, C144, and COV-NY cultures, each of the viral mutants retained approximately equivalent sensitivity to neutralization by an ACE2-Fc fusion protein
source: Moreover, for mutants in RBD sequences that arose in the C121, C135, C144, and COV-NY cultures, each of the viral mutants retained approximately equivalent sensitivity to neutralization by an ACE2-Fc fusion protein, suggesting little or no change in interaction with ACE2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ACE2-Fc neutralization data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The E484K and Q493R mutants that emerged during replication in the presence of C121 or C144 caused apparently complete, or near complete, resistance to both antibodies (IC50 > 10 μg/ml)
source: The E484K and Q493R mutants that emerged during replication in the presence of C121 or C144, both caused apparently complete, or near complete, resistance to both antibodies (IC50 > 10 μg/ml, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The E484K and Q493R mutants retained full sensitivity (IC50 < 10 ng/ml) to C135
source: However, both of these mutants retained full sensitivity (IC50 < 10 ng/ml) to C135.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data

claim: The R346S and N440K mutants that emerged during replication in the presence of C135 were resistant to C135, but retained full sensitivity to both C121 and C144
source: Conversely, the R346S and N440K mutants that emerged during replication in the presence of C135 were resistant to C135, but retained full sensitivity to both C121 and C144 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The K444N, K444T, V445G, V445E, and V445L mutants that arose during replication in the presence of COV-NY plasma conferred partial resistance to C135, with IC50 values ranging from 25 to 700 ng/ml
source: The K444N, K444T, V445G, V445E, and V445L mutants that arose during replication in the presence of COV-NY plasma conferred partial resistance to C135, with IC50 values ranging from 25 to 700 ng/ml, but these mutants retained full sensitivity to both C121 and C144 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The E484K and Q493R trimers exhibited complete, or near complete loss of binding to C121 and C144 antibodies but retained WT levels of binding to C135
source: The E484K and Q493R trimers exhibited complete, or near complete loss of binding to C121 and C144 antibodies but retained WT levels of binding to C135 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The R346S and N440K mutants exhibited complete loss of binding to C135, but retained WT levels of binding to C121 and C144
source: Conversely, the R346S and N440K mutants exhibited complete loss of binding to C135, but retained WT levels of binding to C121 and C144.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data

claim: The K444N and V445E mutants retained near WT levels of binding to all three antibodies, despite exhibiting partial resistance to C135
source: The K444N and V445E mutants retained near WT levels of binding to all three antibodies, despite exhibiting partial resistance to C135 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Mutants N148S, K150R, K150E, S151P exhibited specific resistance to COV-47 plasma with the COV-47 plasma NT50 for these mutants reduced by 8- to 10-fold
source: Analysis of mutants that were isolated from the virus population that emerged during rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replication in the presence of COV-47 plasma (specifically N148S, K150R, K150E, S151P) revealed that these mutants exhibited specific resistance to COV-47 plasma. Indeed, the COV-47 plasma NT50 for these mutants was reduced by 8- to 10-fold (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The antibody or antibodies responsible for majority of neutralizing activity in COV-47 plasma target an NTD epitope that includes amino acids 148–151
source: This finding indicates that the antibody or antibodies responsible for majority of neutralizing activity in COV-47 plasma target an NTD epitope that includes amino acids 148–151, even though the highly potent monoclonal antibody (C144) isolated from COV-47 targets the RBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance pattern of NTD mutants to COV-47 plasma

claim: Viral mutants K444N or T and V445G, E or L conferred substantial resistance to neutralization by COV-NY plasma, with ~ 10 to 30-fold reduction in NT50
source: The viral population that emerged during replication in COV-NY plasma yielded mutants K444N or T and V445G, E or L. Each of these mutations conferred substantial resistance to neutralization by COV-NY plasma, with ~ 10 to 30-fold reduction in NT50 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The dominant neutralizing activity in COV-NY plasma is represented by an antibody or antibodies recognizing an RBD epitope that includes K444 and V445
source: Thus, the dominant neutralizing activity in COV-NY plasma is represented by an antibody or antibodies recognizing an RBD epitope that includes K444 and V445.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance pattern of K444 and V445 mutants to COV-NY plasma

claim: The mutations that conferred complete or near complete resistance to the potent RBD-specific monoclonal antibodies C144, C135, and C121 conferred little or no resistance to neutralization by plasma from the same individual, or other individuals
source: Interestingly, the mutations that conferred complete or near complete resistance to the potent RBD-specific monoclonal antibodies C144, C135, and C121 conferred little or no resistance to neutralization by plasma from the same individual, or other individuals (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Among the 55,189 SARS-CoV-2 sequences in the CoV2-Glue database at the time of writing, 2175 different non-synonymous mutations were present in natural populations of SARS-CoV-2 S protein sequences
source: Among the 55,189 SARS-CoV-2 sequences in the CoV2-Glue database at the time of writing, 2175 different non-synonymous mutations were present in natural populations of SARS-CoV-2 S protein sequences.
evidence: This is based on database analysis of SARS-CoV-2 sequences

claim: Most mutations that arose in the selection experiments were also present in natural viral populations
source: Consistent with the finding that none of the mutations that arose in our selection experiments gave an obvious fitness deficit (in the context of rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP), most were also present in natural viral populations.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental mutations with database sequences

claim: Naturally occurring mutations at positions E484, F490, Q493, and S494 conferred complete or partial resistance to C121 and C144
source: Consistent with, and extending our findings with rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP, naturally occurring mutations at positions E484, F490, Q493, and S494 conferred complete or partial resistance to C121 and C144 (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 7A,C

claim: Naturally occurring mutations that conferred complete or partial resistance to C135 were at positions R346, N439, N440, K444, V445 and G446
source: Naturally occurring mutations that conferred complete or partial resistance to C135 were at positions R346, N439, N440, K444, V445 and G446.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data

claim: Preincubation of S-NanoLuc with a molar excess of C121 or C144 completely blocked binding to 293T/ACE2cl.22 cells
source: Indeed, in experiments where the binding of a conformationally stabilized trimeric S-NanoLuc fusion protein to 293T/ACE2cl.22 cells was measured, preincubation of S-NanoLuc with a molar excess of C121 or C144 completely blocked binding (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Preincubation with C135 only partly blocked binding to 293T/ACE2cl.22 cells
source: Conversely, preincubation with C135 only partly blocked binding to 293T/ACE2cl.22 cells, consistent with the finding that the C135 conformational epitope does not overlap the ACE2 binding site (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 7E and structural analysis in Figure 7D

claim: With one exception (N439K), all antibody resistance mutations uncovered are present in global SARS-CoV-2 at frequencies of < 1 in 1000 sequences
source: With one exception (N439K) that is circulating nearly exclusively in Scotland and is present in ~ 1% of COV-Glue database sequences, (and whose frequency may be overestimated due to regional oversampling) all antibody resistance mutations uncovered herein are present in global SARS-CoV-2 at frequencies of < 1 in 1000 sequences (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on database analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: N439K is circulating nearly exclusively in Scotland and is present in ~ 1% of COV-Glue database sequences
source: With one exception (N439K) that is circulating nearly exclusively in Scotland and is present in ~ 1% of COV-Glue database sequences, (and whose frequency may be overestimated due to regional oversampling) all antibody resistance mutations uncovered herein are present in global SARS-CoV-2 at frequencies of < 1 in 1000 sequences (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on database analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replication in the presence of mixtures of C121+C135 or C144+C135 led to sparse infection of individual cells in p1 cultures, but there was little or no formation of foci
source: Conversely, rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP replication in the presence of mixtures of C121+C135 or C144+C135 led to sparse infection of individual cells in p1 cultures, but there was little or no formation of foci that would suggest propagation of infection from these infected cells (Figure 9A–C)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9A–C

claim: No replication-competent rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was detected in p2 cultures established with mixtures of C121+C135 or C144+C135
source: Consequently, viral spread was apparently completely suppressed and no replication-competent rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was detected in p2 cultures established with mixtures of the two antibodies (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 9D

claim: Peak viral burden in swabs and sputum approximately corresponds with the onset of symptoms, and clearly occurs before seroconversion
source: Peak viral burden in swabs and sputum, which likely corresponds to peak infectiousness and frequency of transmission events, appears to approximately correspond with the onset of symptoms, and clearly occurs before seroconversion (Wölfel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wölfel et al., 2020

claim: Most transmission events likely involve virus populations that are yet to experience antibody-imposed selective pressure in the transmitting individual
source: Thus, it is quite plausible that most transmission events involve virus populations that are yet to experience antibody-imposed selective pressure in the transmitting individual.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of peak viral burden relative to seroconversion

claim: Neutralizing antibody titers among COVID-19 convalescents are extremely variable
source: Millions of individuals have already been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and among them, neutralizing antibody titers are extremely variable (Robbiani et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b; Luchsinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: Related, potently neutralizing monoclonal antibodies that recognize the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) are often elicited in SARS-CoV-2 infection
source: Recent studies have shown that related, potently neutralizing monoclonal antibodies that recognize the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) are often elicited in SARS-CoV-2 infection (Robbiani et al., 2020; Brouwer et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020a; Wec et al., 2020; Kreer et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2020; Ju et al., 2020; Seydoux et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Zost et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: A significant fraction of COVID19 convalescents exhibit low levels of plasma neutralizing activity
source: Paradoxically, a significant fraction of COVID19 convalescents, including some from whom potent neutralizing antibodies have been cloned, exhibit low levels of plasma neutralizing activity (Robbiani et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b; Luchsinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: Natural SARS-CoV-2 infection may often fail to induce sufficient B-cell expansion and maturation to generate high-titer neutralizing antibodies
source: Together, these findings suggest that natural SARS-CoV-2 infection may often fail to induce sufficient B-cell expansion and maturation to generate high-titer neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many convalescents have low neutralizing antibody titers despite the ability to clone potent antibodies from some individuals

claim: Coronaviruses encode a 3'−5' exonuclease activity that provides a proofreading function that enhances replication fidelity and limits viral sequence diversification
source: The exonuclease activity provides a proofreading function that enhances replication fidelity and limits viral sequence diversification (Denison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denison et al., 2011

claim: The inter-individual variation in SARS-CoV-2 sequences is low compared to many other RNA viruses
source: Notably, the inter-individual variation in SARS-CoV-2 sequences is low compared to many other RNA viruses (van Dorp et al., 2020; Rambaut et al., 2020; Dearlove et al., 2020; Rausch et al., 2020), in part because coronaviruses encode a 3'−5' exonuclease activity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: A single swab from an infected individual can contain in excess of 109 copies of viral RNA
source: Many millions of individuals have been infected by SARS-CoV-2, and a single swab from an infected individual can contain in excess of 109 copies of viral RNA (Wölfel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wölfel et al., 2020

claim: SARS-CoV-2 genomes encoding every possible single amino-acid substitution are present in the global population
source: It follows that SARS-CoV-2 genomes encoding every possible single amino-acid substitution are present in the global population, and perhaps in a significant fraction of individual COVID19 patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the large population size and high viral loads

claim: Functional SARS-CoV-2 S protein variants with mutations in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and N-terminal domain that confer resistance to monoclonal antibodies or convalescent plasma can be readily selected
source: Using a recombinant chimeric VSV/SARS-CoV-2 reporter virus, we show that functional SARS-CoV-2 S protein variants with mutations in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and N-terminal domain that confer resistance to monoclonal antibodies or convalescent plasma can be readily selected.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the selection experiments described throughout

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S variants that resist commonly elicited neutralizing antibodies are now present at low frequencies in circulating SARS-CoV-2 populations
source: Notably, SARS-CoV-2 S variants that resist commonly elicited neutralizing antibodies are now present at low frequencies in circulating SARS-CoV-2 populations.
evidence: This is based on database analysis of circulating SARS-CoV-2 sequences

claim: The emergence of antibody-resistant SARS-CoV-2 variants that might limit the therapeutic usefulness of monoclonal antibodies can be mitigated by the use of antibody combinations that target distinct neutralizing epitopes
source: Finally, the emergence of antibody-resistant SARS-CoV-2 variants that might limit the therapeutic usefulness of monoclonal antibodies can be mitigated by the use of antibody combinations that target distinct neutralizing epitopes.
evidence: This is supported by the combination antibody experiments showing suppression of escape mutants

claim: C135 does not compete with C121 and C144 for binding to the RBD
source: These results are also consistent with experiments which indicated that C135 does not compete with C121 and C144 for binding to the RBD (Robbiani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robbiani et al., 2020

claim: C135 might inhibit S-ACE-2 binding by steric interference with access to the ACE two binding site
source: C135 might inhibit S-ACE-2 binding by steric interference with access to the ACE two binding site.
evidence: This is speculated based on the partial blocking of ACE2 binding and the location of the C135 epitope

claim: The C121 and C144 neutralizing epitopes appear to be similar, and include E484 and Q493
source: The C121 and C144 neutralizing epitopes appear to be similar, and include E484 and Q493, while a clearly distinct conformational epitope seems to be recognized by C135, that includes R346 and N440 residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping resistance mutations for C121 and C144

claim: A clearly distinct conformational epitope is recognized by C135, that includes R346 and N440 residues
source: The C121 and C144 neutralizing epitopes appear to be similar, and include E484 and Q493, while a clearly distinct conformational epitope seems to be recognized by C135, that includes R346 and N440 residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct resistance mutations for C135

claim: Antibodies that constitute at least part of the neutralizing activity evident in COV-NY plasma appear to recognize an epitope that includes K444 and V445
source: Antibodies that constitute at least part of the neutralizing activity evident in COV-NY plasma appear to recognize an epitope that includes and K444 and V445.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance mutations selected by COV-NY plasma

claim: The ability of mutations at K444 and V445 to confer partial resistance to C135 is consistent with their spatial proximity to the C135 conformational epitope
source: The ability of mutations at these residues to confer partial resistance to C135 is consistent with their spatial proximity to the C135 conformational epitope (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The loss of affinity of K444N and V445E mutants for C135 was sufficient to impart partial neutralization resistance but insufficient to abolish binding in the solution binding assay
source: Presumably the loss of affinity of these mutants for C135 was sufficient to impart partial neutralization resistance but insufficient to abolish binding in the solution binding assay.
evidence: This is speculated to explain the discrepancy between neutralization and binding assays

claim: Potent neutralizing antibodies based on IGHV3-53 have been isolated from COVID19 convalescents
source: The low levels of somatic hypermutation and repetitive manner in which similar antibodies (e.g. those based on IGHV3-53 Robbiani et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020) have been isolated from COVID19 convalescents suggests that potently neutralizing responses should be readily elicited.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: The low levels of somatic hypermutation and repetitive manner in which similar antibodies have been isolated from COVID19 convalescents suggests that potently neutralizing responses should be readily elicited
source: The low levels of somatic hypermutation and repetitive manner in which similar antibodies (e.g. those based on IGHV3-53 Robbiani et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020) have been isolated from COVID19 convalescents suggests that potently neutralizing responses should be readily elicited.
evidence: This is inferred from the characteristics of isolated antibodies

claim: Neutralizing antibodies are a key component of adaptive immunity against many viruses that can be elicited by natural infection or vaccination
source: Neutralizing antibodies are a key component of adaptive immunity against many viruses that can be elicited by natural infection or vaccination (Plotkin, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation

claim: Passively administered antibodies are currently among the most promising therapeutic and prophylactic antiviral agents against SARS-CoV-2
source: Indeed, interventions to interrupt SARS-CoV-2 replication and spread are urgently sought, and passively administered antibodies are currently among the most promising therapeutic and prophylactic antiviral agents.
evidence: This reflects the state of therapeutic development at the time of writing
